4 Swiss Re Institute sigma No 1/2025  
Key takeaways
Losses from primary perils remain an ever present risk and drive most deviations from trend
While losses from both primary and secondary perils are on an upward trajectory, history shows that annual losses from primary perils 
vary considerably from year-to-year, punctuated by peak loss years. In the past 30 years, there have been five such years where losses 
from primary perils were more than double the trend (>100% on X-axis). These years also happen to be years in terms of global losses 
from all natural catastrophe events were highest, affirming the strong influence of primary-peril losses. 
Distribution of annual losses from primary and secondary perils in % deviation from trend (1995 ‒ 2024)
Source: Swiss Re Institute

Exposure to natural catastrophe risks a key factor in driving claims costs 
Analysis of the link between catastrophe losses per policy and homeowner insurance prices at state level shows a strong correlation. 
States with highest exposures to natural catastrophes risks (according to insurance loss history), are also where, in general, 
homeowner premiums are highest. In states with higher average premiums, extremely high premium levels are localised. Like in 
Florida, for instance, where average premium per policy is amongst the highest of all states. In 11% of the Florida’s zip codes, premiums 
per policy were above USD 10 000. These are typically coastal zip codes with highest risk of storm surge and/or wind damage. 
Distribution of premium per policy in Florida at zip-code level, USD, 2022
Source: FIO Data, Swiss Re Institute
